text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Swedish industry saw one of its most profitable years in 1995, according to a study by Statistics Sweden.
- Astra says its new asthma medication will change the treatment of asthma and cut the need to use various medications currently on the market, but Glaxo disagrees.
- Warning signs of the dangers of smoking are inadequate on Swedish tobacco packaging, according to Sweden's defence research institute (FAO).
- Sweden's Prime Minister Goran Persson says the state is to build 15,000 student flats.
- The Swedish pensioners' party, founded in 1987, has started to prepare itself for the 1998 general election and will be a force to be reckoned with, political analysts say.
- Four out of five Swedish households believe the government will put forward more cut back measures in the next budget and living standards will fall, a survey shows.
- Under a Swedish legal change companies facing bankruptcy can chose to be reorganised so that they have a change to start over and return to profitability.
- Two partly owned Swedish companies, Pharmacia & Upjohn and Asea Brown Boveri, have together contributed $50,000 to candidates in the U.S. presidential race.

- Swedish forest products companies may be able to win back some of the fines they have paid if things go their way in the European Union's court. Eight companies were fined five million crowns each more then 10 years ago after being found guilty of colluding in the setting of pulp prices.
